title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Right ventricular myocardial infarction (RVMI) occurs when an abrupt reduction or cessation of coronary blood flow causes irreversible necrosis of the right ventricular myocardium. Most cases result from proximal right coronary artery occlusion, with less frequent causes including left circumflex artery obstruction or profound systemic hypotension. Established risk factors mirror those of atherosclerotic coronary artery disease, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, tobacco use, and advanced age. Right ventricular ischemia impairs preload-dependent cardiac output, reduces left ventricular filling, and may lead to systemic hypotension or cardiogenic shock. Clinical features often resemble left-sided myocardial infarction, with chest pain, dyspnea, nausea, dizziness, and hypotension, while elevated jugular venous pressure with clear lung fields suggests right ventricular involvement. Diagnosis relies on electrocardiography with right-sided precordial leads, cardiac biomarkers, and imaging as indicated, and management emphasizes prompt reperfusion, cautious preload optimization, and avoidance of preload-reducing agents. Complications include arrhythmias, shock, and mechanical dysfunction, and prognosis depends on infarct size, hemodynamic compromise, and timeliness of intervention.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity enhances clinician competence in evaluating and managing RVMI, emphasizing recognition of clinical presentation, interpretation of right-sided electrocardiographic changes, and integration of biomarkers and imaging findings into timely diagnostic decisions. Participants learn evidence-based reperfusion strategies, hemodynamic optimization, and strategies to prevent complications, including arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock. Collaboration within an interprofessional team, including cardiology clinicians, critical care staff, and nursing personnel, promotes coordinated care, timely intervention, and improved patient outcomes through shared monitoring, treatment planning, and safe post-infarction management.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate right from left ventricular myocardial infarction based on clinical presentation and electrocardiographic findings. Identify indications for atrioventricular pacing in individuals experiencing right ventricular myocardial infarction. Implement evidence-based, individualized strategies for managing right ventricular myocardial infarction and mitigating its potential complications. Collaborate with all members of the interprofessional team, including specialists such as cardiologists, emergency medicine clinicians, and critical care practitioners, to provide efficient, comprehensive, and coordinated treatment for patients with right ventricular myocardial infarction. title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Introduction
content: Right ventricular myocardial infarction (RVMI) most commonly results from atherosclerotic plaque rupture and occlusion of the right coronary artery in a right-dominant circulation. Occlusion of the left circumflex artery may also cause RVMI. This condition is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. [1] Prompt clinical diagnosis guides management in critically ill individuals. RVMI should be suspected in all individuals with inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), complicating at least 40% of cases. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) increasingly demonstrates that RVMI also occurs in many anterior STEMI cases. Isolated RVMI remains uncommon. This activity addresses the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of RVMI.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Etiology
content: RVMI is most frequently caused by atherosclerotic disease. The proximal right coronary artery serves as the culprit vessel in right-dominant circulations, accounting for approximately 85% of cases. Less commonly, atherosclerotic plaque rupture in the left circumflex artery causes RVMI in left-dominant systems, accounting for roughly 15% of cases. Additional causes include coronary thromboembolism, coronary artery spasm or dissection, and blunt chest trauma to the supplying vessel. Rarely, anomalous coronary artery anatomy precipitates right ventricular ischemia. Prolonged systemic hypotension can also reduce right ventricular perfusion, resulting in ischemia.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Epidemiology
content: The incidence of RVMI coexisting with inferior wall left ventricular dysfunction ranges from 10% to 50%, reflecting challenges in identification in living patients. Autopsy study results demonstrate higher rates. Isolated infarction or dysfunction of the right ventricle is rare but may result from iatrogenic injury during interventional procedures or cardiac surgery.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Epidemiology
content: Transient right ventricular stunning further limits detection. In a recent single-center retrospective study of 500 patients presenting with STEMI, at least 16% demonstrated electrocardiographic or echocardiographic evidence of right ventricular involvement. [2] A multicenter study of 242 patients with STEMI using cardiac MRI identified right ventricular edema in 51% and late gadolinium enhancement in 31%. [3]

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Pathophysiology
content: The right ventricle receives arterial blood primarily from the right coronary artery (RCA), which originates from the right coronary cusp of the aorta. The first division gives rise to the conus artery, which supplies the right ventricular outflow tract. The RCA also supplies the sinoatrial node.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Pathophysiology
content: Traveling within the atrioventricular groove, the RCA gives off multiple small branches to the anterior right ventricle before terminating in the acute marginal branch, which courses along the anterior diaphragm, and the posterior descending artery, which runs posteriorly. The posterior descending artery supplies the atrioventricular node in 90% of patients, with the left circumflex supplying it in the remaining 10%. This artery also perfuses the inferior wall of both ventricles and represents a terminal branch of the RCA in 85% of patients, arising from the left coronary circulation in 15%. Occlusion of the proximal or middle segment of the RCA is the primary cause of RVMI.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Pathophysiology
content: The principal consequence of right ventricular ischemia and infarction is impaired contractility, leading to reduced venous return to the lungs, diminished left ventricular preload, and decreased cardiac output, resulting in hypotension, cardiogenic shock, and reduced pulmonary blood flow. Increased right atrial and ventricular pressures cause systemic congestion, while lungs remain clear. Right ventricular dilation alters interventricular septal motion and function, and this effect is exacerbated when left ventricular ischemia occurs concurrently. Leftward septal shift during diastole impedes left ventricular filling, further reducing cardiac output, a phenomenon termed "loss of biventricular interdependence."

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical
content: Patients with RVMI may exhibit symptoms typical of left-sided infarction, including chest pain with or without radiation, dyspnea, nausea, and dizziness. Conduction disturbances can range from bradycardia to complete heart block, and hypotension occurs more frequently in this population. Signs of right heart failure, such as acute peripheral edema and jugular venous distention (JVD), may also be present.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical
content: The classic triad of JVD, clear lung fields, and hypotension characterizes right ventricular dysfunction. A pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border may indicate tricuspid regurgitation, although lower right heart filling pressures often render the murmur inaudible. Rare third (S3) or fourth (S4) heart sounds generated by the right ventricle may be appreciated at the left lower sternal border and increase with inspiration. More than 30% of patients with inferior wall myocardial infarction have right ventricular involvement, but only 10% develop significant hemodynamic compromise. [4] [5] Marked sensitivity to preload-reducing agents, including nitrates, morphine, or diuretics, suggests hemodynamically significant right ventricular dysfunction. [6]

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Electrocardiography
content: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is the first diagnostic test performed in patients presenting with chest pain. Inferior lead ischemia or infarction in leads II, III, and arteriovenous fistula  indicates left ventricular involvement (see Image . Electrocardiogram Showing Inferior ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction With Right Ventricular Involvement). ST elevation in lead III greater than lead II is highly suggestive of RVMI and should prompt evaluation with right-sided ECG. ST elevation in lead V1 is also indicative of RVMI, particularly when accompanied by ST depression in lead V2. ST elevation in V1 greater than V2 further supports the diagnosis.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Electrocardiography
content: A conventional left-sided ECG has limited sensitivity for detecting right ventricular ischemia because the right ventricle is anterior. When right ventricular involvement is suspected, a right-sided ECG offers the highest sensitivity and specificity. ST elevation in V4R greater than 1.0 mm demonstrates 100% sensitivity, 87% specificity, and 92% predictive accuracy. Conduction abnormalities, including right bundle branch block, bradycardia, or complete heart block, may appear on the ECG but are sometimes nonspecific. An isoelectric ST segment in V1 combined with markedly depressed ST in V2 also suggests RVMI. [7] [8] [9] [10]

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Cardiac Enzymes
content: Cardiac biomarkers will be elevated in RVMI, similarly to left ventricular infarction. However, when differentiating between hemodynamically significant pulmonary embolism and RVMI, the picture is not as clear, as both troponin-I and creatine kinase–myocardial band levels may be elevated in a minority of cases of significant pulmonary embolism.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Chest Radiography
content: Chest radiography also has limited specificity and diagnostic capability. Findings of an enlarged cardiac silhouette, inferior or superior vena cava dilation, and clear lung fields may be noted. The presence or absence of pulmonary edema may help evaluate concomitant left ventricular dysfunction or further assess the likelihood of a pulmonary embolus.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Echocardiography
content: Echocardiography has a high threshold for detecting right-sided myocardial dysfunction. The increasing availability and resolution of this imaging technique have established it as a valuable diagnostic modality in settings such as the emergency department and the operating room. Sensitivity and specificity may reach 82% and 93%, respectively, for the detection of RVMI.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Echocardiography
content: Findings may include right ventricular wall dyskinesia, hypokinesia, or akinesia; paradoxical septal motion secondary to increased right ventricular pressure or volume; reduced tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion; tricuspid regurgitation; and pulmonary regurgitation. The myocardial performance index (MPI) is calculated as the sum of isovolumic contraction time and isovolumic relaxation time divided by ejection time, as shown in the following equation: MPI = (isovolumic contraction time + isovolumic relaxation time) / ejection time

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Echocardiography
content: MPI values of 0.30 or greater are associated with RVMI. [11] Echocardiography can also aid in differentiating right ventricular dysfunction from other causes, including pulmonary embolism, detect complications of RVMI, and provide prognostic information by assessing right ventricular function and global longitudinal strain. Serial studies allow evaluation of recovery or progression.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Cardiac Catheterization
content: Cardiac catheterization and hemodynamic assessment provide direct evaluation of right ventricular function in RVMI. Findings may include elevated right atrial pressure and equalization of right atrial pressure with pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Pulmonary artery pressures are often low due to reduced right ventricular output. Cardiac output and cardiac index are also decreased. The Kussmaul sign, marked by an increase in jugular venous pressure during inspiration, may be observed. Ventriculography can reveal hypokinesia or akinesia of the right ventricular free wall. Coronary angiography frequently demonstrates occlusion or severe stenosis of the proximal RCA, commonly involving the right ventricular branch.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging
content: Cardiac MRI in RVMI typically demonstrates right ventricular dilatation, abnormal right ventricular wall motion, paradoxical septal motion, and tricuspid regurgitation. T2-weighted imaging identifies myocardial edema, whereas late gadolinium enhancement sequences reveal transmural injury. Evidence indicates a discrepancy between RVMIs detected on autopsy and those identified by conventional modalities such as echocardiography.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging
content: MRI provides an ideal tool for assessing both acute and chronic RVMI. In anterior myocardial infarction, the anterior or anterolateral portion of the right ventricular free wall, along with the right ventricular apex, is involved, with an incidence of 33%. In an inferior wall myocardial infarction, the inferior or inferolateral portion of the right ventricular free wall is affected. Rarely, isolated RVMI caused by occlusion of a nondominant RCA or branch vessel involves the lateral and inferior right ventricular free wall.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management
content: Management of RVMI focuses on optimizing preload, maintaining hemodynamic stability, and treating the underlying ischemia. Key principles are explained below.
contents: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management. Management of RVMI focuses on optimizing preload, maintaining hemodynamic stability, and treating the underlying ischemia. Key principles are explained below.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Volume Optimization
content: Clinically significant right ventricular dysfunction may reduce left ventricular preload, decrease cardiac output, and precipitate systemic hypotension. Management of suspected RVMI may include a 500 mL crystalloid fluid challenge. Hemodynamic response should be carefully monitored, as patients may present with variable intravascular volume status ranging from hypovolemia to fluid overload. Fluids should be titrated to achieve a jugular venous pressure of 10 to 12 cm H2O, because excessive volume can impair right ventricular output by displacing the ventricle from the Frank-Starling curve. Agents that cause venodilation, including nitrates and diuretics, should be avoided. [12] [13] [14]

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Volume Optimization
content: Pharmacologic therapy with inotropic agents may be indicated when the hemodynamic response to fluids is suboptimal. Dobutamine is the most extensively studied agent and has been shown to improve cardiac index and right ventricular stroke volume. Dobutamine also enhances left ventricular function, promoting forward flow. The combination of inhaled nitric oxide with dobutamine further reduces pulmonary vascular resistance, thereby decreasing right ventricular afterload and myocardial work.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Volume Optimization
content: Milrinone, a phosphodiesterase III inhibitor, may also improve right ventricular dysfunction. Increased cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels from milrinone administration enhance right ventricular contractility and reduce pulmonary vascular resistance. However, milrinone is not a selective pulmonary vasodilator, and its use carries the risk of exacerbating systemic hypotension.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Volume Optimization
content: Calcium sensitizers may also improve right ventricular function, although their use is currently limited to European centers. One such agent, levosimendan, improves right ventricular function by increasing myocyte sensitivity to intracellular calcium without raising calcium concentrations. [15] Clinical effects include enhanced inotropy and peripheral vasodilation.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Pharmacologic Management
content: Pharmacological therapy for acute coronary syndrome in the setting of RVMI includes dual antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, β-blockers, and renin-angiotensin system inhibition. Dual antiplatelet therapy consists of aspirin combined with a P2Y12 inhibitor, such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor. Anticoagulation is provided with unfractionated heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or thrombolysis. β-blockers should be administered cautiously and selectively in patients who are hemodynamically stable without evidence of right ventricular failure, hypotension, or bradycardia. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers may be considered in stable patients to improve clinical outcomes.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Revascularization Strategies
content: The timing of reperfusion is the primary determinant of survival and myocardial recovery, as in left ventricular infarction. Early intervention is preferred. Primary PCI provides the best outcomes. Thrombolytic therapy is an alternative if primary PCI is not available within the recommended time frame.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Arrhythmia Control
content: Temporary pacing may be required to treat bradycardia or atrioventricular block. The anatomic proximity of the cardiac conduction system to the right ventricle predisposes patients with RVMI to arrhythmias ranging from bradycardia to complete heart block. Reduced right ventricular preload and relatively fixed left ventricular stroke volume render systemic cardiac output rate-dependent. Evidence demonstrates that atrioventricular pacing improves survival in RVMI complicated by complete heart block, whereas isolated ventricular pacing does not.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Mechanical Support for Right and Left Ventricular Dysfunction
content: Patients with concurrent left ventricular dysfunction may benefit from afterload reduction with an intra-aortic balloon pump, which augments left ventricular function, increases diastolic flow, and improves coronary perfusion, thereby increasing right ventricular blood flow. Rarely, a right ventricular assist device must be implanted.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Several conditions can mimic the presentation of RVMI, producing chest pain, hypotension, or hemodynamic instability. The following list includes key differential diagnoses to consider when evaluating patients suspected of having this condition: Acute aortic dissection Acute cholecystitis Acute gastritis Acute mitral regurgitation Acute pericarditis Anxiety disorders Aortic dissection Aortic stenosis Asthma Biliary disease Cardiogenic shock

content: Clinical, hemodynamic, and diagnostic clues, such as right-sided congestion in RVMI versus hypotension without jugular venous distention in other causes, facilitate differentiation from other acute presentations. Recognizing these differences is essential to implementing appropriate interventions and optimizing survival.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Prognosis
content: Prognosis in RVMI depends on multiple factors. Favorable prognostic indicators include timely revascularization, isolated RVMI, and hemodynamic stability. Poor prognostic factors include delayed revascularization, hemodynamic instability, significant left ventricular involvement, high-grade atrioventricular block, and tachyarrhythmias. Inferior wall myocardial infarctions complicated by RVMI carry a worse prognosis than either condition alone. In patients without right ventricular failure, in-hospital 30-day mortality is 4.4% with thrombolytic therapy and 3.2% with PCI, increasing to 13% and 8.3%, respectively, when right ventricular failure is present.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Prognosis
content: Mortality in cardiogenic shock reaches 100% with thrombolysis and 44% with PCI. Isolated RVMI demonstrates lower mortality rates of 5% to 10% when treated promptly. [16] Short-term prognosis in RVMI is worse than in isolated left ventricular infarction, with increased in-hospital morbidity and mortality due to critical complications requiring additional interventions, including the use of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, ventricular assist devices, or arrhythmia therapy. Long-term outcomes after hospital discharge and resolution of RVMI are comparable to those of patients with left ventricular myocardial infarction.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Complications
content: RVMI can lead to multiple hemodynamic and electrical complications. Mechanical sequelae include ventricular septal rupture and tricuspid regurgitation due to papillary muscle rupture or annular dilatation. Electrical disturbances include bradyarrhythmias, ranging from vagally mediated slowing to varying degrees of atrioventricular block, and tachyarrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia, reflecting the susceptibility of the conduction system supplied by the RCA. Hemodynamic consequences include systemic hypotension from ventricular interdependence and hypoxemia secondary to right-to-left shunting. Early recognition of these complications is critical, as prompt intervention can reduce morbidity and improve survival.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: The general population should recognize warning signs of a heart attack, including chest pain, shortness of breath, and nausea. Seek immediate emergency care by calling 911 when these symptoms occur. RVMI is frequently associated with inferior wall myocardial infarctions due to RCA occlusion.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Prescribed medications play a key role in preventing future cardiac events, with adherence to antiplatelets, statins, and other therapies shown to reduce mortality risk. Maintaining a heart-healthy lifestyle, including a healthy diet, regular exercise, stress management, and avoiding smoking or excessive alcohol use, is essential. Family members should learn cardiopulmonary resuscitation and strategies to support recovery after a cardiac event.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: The diagnosis of RVMI, particularly in the absence of acute hemodynamic changes or shock, requires a high index of suspicion. Initial evaluation of patients presenting with chest pain may not reveal evolving ischemia in the right ventricle. Alternative etiologies, including pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, and hypovolemia, can obscure the clinical picture. Noninvasive diagnostic modalities, such as echocardiography, can detect right ventricular dysfunction earlier than conventional tests for myocardial ischemia.

title: Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The diagnosis and management of RVMI are complex and require an interprofessional team, including cardiologists, emergency clinicians, critical care specialists, nurse practitioners, and cardiac rehabilitation specialists. Each team member contributes to addressing the acute event, preventing complications, and promoting long-term recovery. Most patients present with risk factors for coronary artery disease, necessitating emphasis on weight control, smoking cessation, regular exercise, medication adherence, and cholesterol management. Patient and family involvement in treatment decisions is essential, with emphasis on compliance with therapy and follow-up. [17] [18]
